items.title: Thalamic oscillations distinguish natural states of consciousness in humans
items.summary: Direct recordings in a human clinical sample identified a roughly 19–45 Hz central-thalamic rhythm during wakefulness and REM sleep, absent during non-REM sleep in these recordings. The result offers a target for studying how deep brain systems regulate states. It is an association in the studied conditions, not a universal test for conscious experience; non-REM sleep can also include experience.
items.headline: Thalamic recordings reveal a rhythm associated with wakefulness and REM sleep

explainer.finding: A rhythm in a deep brain structure differed between recorded waking, REM, and non-REM states in a human clinical sample.
explainer.method: Researchers compared direct central-thalamic recordings across those states and identified activity around 19–45 Hz during wakefulness and REM in their data.
explainer.meaning: A state-linked rhythm can give researchers a target for testing how brain systems regulate waking and sleep—much as a useful indicator helps locate a process to investigate.
explainer.limits: Tracking these states does not establish a universal consciousness test. The sample and recording conditions matter, and experience can occur during non-REM sleep.

items.title: The act of detecting a stimulus contaminates measures of conscious experience with decision biases
items.authors: Nicolás Sánchez-Fuenzalida, Chris Jungerius, Stephen M. Fleming
items.summary: Experiments with 505 participants combined detection judgments and reproductions of faint visual stimuli. Changes in base rates and rewards affected response criteria, while attention affected a modeled perceptual component. Adding detection judgments also influenced reproduction reports. The study shows why reporting a signal and experiencing it need careful separation; its decomposition depends on the model and tasks used.
items.headline: Saying whether a faint image appeared can change how perception is measured

explainer.finding: A person’s decision to report a faint image can affect measurements intended to describe their visual experience.
explainer.method: Experiments with 505 participants combined detection judgments and stimulus reproductions, varying factors such as rewards, base rates, and attention.
explainer.meaning: Saying “yes, I saw it” can reflect both sensory information and how willing someone is to risk a false alarm. Separating those helps prevent a decision change from being called a perceptual change.
explainer.limits: The separation relies on the tasks and model used. The study does not supply an assumption-free way to measure subjective experience.

items.title: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness
items.summary: The consortium preregistered competing predictions and measured brain activity while 256 people viewed clearly visible stimuli. Results matched some predictions and challenged key commitments of both integrated information and global neuronal workspace theories. The work tests specified claims about visual experience; it neither settles consciousness nor establishes a different theory by elimination.
items.headline: A joint experiment challenges predictions from two consciousness theories

explainer.finding: A shared experiment supported some predictions and challenged important commitments of two consciousness theories.
explainer.method: Advocates agreed on divergent predictions in advance, and the consortium recorded brain activity while 256 people viewed clearly visible stimuli.
explainer.meaning: Agreeing on the test beforehand makes it harder for each group to select only favorable results afterward. The mismatches identify where theories need clearer explanations and fresh predictions.
explainer.limits: These are tests of specified claims about visual experience. They do not settle consciousness as a whole or prove another theory true by elimination.

items.title: Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex
items.summary: The project paired calcium imaging of about 75,000 neurons with electron-microscopy reconstructions containing more than 200,000 cells and roughly half a billion synapses. Researchers can investigate how measured responses relate to physical connections in visual cortex. This is an open resource from one mouse, with reconstruction and sampling limits; a wiring diagram does not by itself explain a mind.
items.headline: A mouse-brain dataset links neural activity with detailed wiring

explainer.finding: An open mouse-brain dataset connects recorded neural responses with an unusually detailed reconstruction of physical wiring.
explainer.method: The project paired calcium imaging of about 75,000 neurons with electron-microscopy reconstructions containing more than 200,000 cells and roughly half a billion synapses.
explainer.meaning: A road map and a record of traffic answer different questions. Having both helps researchers investigate how connections relate to activity.
explainer.limits: The resource comes from one mouse and contains sampling and reconstruction limits. Wiring plus recorded activity does not by itself explain every computation or experience.

items.title: A streaming brain-to-voice neuroprosthesis to restore naturalistic communication
items.summary: In one clinical-trial participant with severe paralysis, a system used cortical surface recordings and trained neural networks to synthesize speech in a continuous stream. Decoding proceeded in 80-millisecond increments. The demonstration targets attempted speech under a specialized recording and training setup; it does not establish general thought reading or equivalent performance across people.
items.headline: A trained brain interface turns attempted speech into streaming audio

explainer.finding: A trained brain interface converted one participant’s attempted speech into continuously generated audio.
explainer.method: The system used cortical surface recordings and trained neural networks, decoding in 80-millisecond increments in a clinical-trial participant with severe paralysis.
explainer.meaning: Streaming can reduce the need to wait for an entire attempted utterance before hearing output, an important feature for conversational turn-taking.
explainer.limits: This specialized, trained setup targets attempted speech. It does not establish unrestricted thought reading or the same performance in other people.

items.title: Sleep microstructure organizes memory replay
items.authors: Hongyu Chang, Wenbo Tang et al.
items.summary: Simultaneous neural recordings and pupil measurements distinguished non-REM sleep substates associated with replay of recent versus older experiences. Disrupting sharp-wave ripples in the recent-memory-associated substate impaired later recall. The experiment links timing to a memory effect in mice; it is not evidence that monitoring or changing human pupil size can improve learning.
items.headline: Mouse sleep substates separate replay of recent and older memories

explainer.finding: Different substates of mouse non-REM sleep were associated with replay of recent and older experiences.
explainer.method: Researchers recorded neural activity and pupils, then disrupted sharp-wave ripples in the substate linked to recent memories; later recall was impaired.
explainer.meaning: The intervention connects the timing of neural events with a memory outcome. It helps explain why treating all of sleep as one uniform state can miss useful structure.
explainer.limits: This is evidence from mice under specific conditions. It does not show that changing human pupil size or using a consumer sleep tracker improves learning.

items.title: Quantifying the prevalence and impact of overreaching causal claims in social science
items.headline: Causal wording changes how readers interpret correlational studies
items.authors: Calvin Isch, Timothy Dörr, Neil Fasching, Grace Jennings, Duncan J. Watts
items.summary: A corpus analysis found frequent causal wording in cross-sectional research. Separate reader experiments showed that phrasing affects interpretation. Classification and sampling constrain the prevalence estimate.

evidence.question: Does wording overstate causal evidence?
evidence.method: Validated text classification and reader experiments.
evidence.limitations: The selected corpus does not represent every study design.

explainer.finding: Causal language can strengthen readers’ causal interpretations.
explainer.method: Readers encountered original or associationally rewritten abstracts.
explainer.limits: Corpus prevalence depends on classification; experimental results concern the tested reading tasks.

editorialReview.reason: Primary study followed from a research briefing; separates corpus analysis from reader experiments.
